title: The moonlit ride
hookLine: King Ajatasattu, who killed his father, rides out on a full-moon night to ask what practice is good for

lines: A KING WHO KILLED HIS FATHER.
cards: It's the full moon of the autumn month, an observance night.
King Ajatasattu of Magadha sits on the upper terrace of his palace at Rajagaha, among his ministers, and says something almost tender: how lovely this moonlit night is.
Which teacher could we visit tonight who might bring peace to my heart? Later in this discourse, the king will confess what he's carrying.
Tradition says he seized the throne and had his own father, King Bimbisara, put to death. That's the man looking at the moon.

teach.b: One by one, his ministers suggest well-known teachers. Six of them. The king says nothing.
One man on the terrace is silent too: Jivaka, the royal physician. Why so quiet, Jivaka?

teach.h: JIVAKA: GO TO MY MANGO GROVE
teach.b: The Blessed One is staying in my mango grove, Jivaka says, with twelve hundred and fifty monks. Go and see him. So the king rides out: five hundred women on she-elephants, torches burning, the king on the royal elephant.
Near the grove, he's suddenly afraid; his hair stands on end. Jivaka, are you handing me to my enemies?

teach.h: NOT ONE SNEEZE, NOT ONE COUGH
teach.b: How can there be twelve hundred and fifty monks here, and not one sneeze, not one cough? Don't be afraid, great king, says Jivaka. Look, there are lamps burning in the pavilion.
The king walks in and sees the whole community sitting utterly still, like a clear lake. I wish my son, Prince Udayibhadda, could have a calm like this, he says. Then he bows and asks his question.
People in every trade get a visible fruit from their work: elephant riders, archers, cooks, barbers, bath attendants. They support their families with it.
Can you show me a fruit of the contemplative life, visible here and now?

That's the question the whole discourse answers. The Pali for the night he rode out is uposatha: the observance day, at the moon's turning. A troubled king, on a holy night, asking what practice is actually good for.

how: Uposatha, the observance day at the new and full moons (and in some traditions the quarter moons), is still kept in Theravada communities, when lay people often visit monasteries, take precepts and listen to teachings.

o: the observance day, at the moon's turning
a night spent with no sleep at all

games.q: the moonlit ride: tap the pairs.
p: the royal physician, silent at first
where the monks sat in silence
the observance day at the moon's turning

s: the king rode straight to the Buddha without hesitation
near the grove he grew afraid and asked Jivaka if he was being betrayed.
the king was frightened by the silence of twelve hundred and fifty monks
not one sneeze, not one cough, so he suspected a trap.
the king's question compares the monk's life to ordinary trades
cooks, archers and barbers see a fruit of their work; what fruit does the contemplative see?

games.q: you're the king, riding into a dark grove where twelve hundred and fifty people are supposed to be, and there's no sound at all. what do you do?
o: ask Jivaka if he's deceiving you.
call for the guards to search the grove.
games.why: the king asks Jivaka, hair standing on end, whether he's being betrayed. Jivaka points to the lamps in the pavilion, and the king walks in.

practice: Ask the king's question for yourself, honestly: is there a fruit of your practice you can see here and now, a little more patience, a quicker return from anger, a quieter night?
Maybe nothing obvious yet, and either answer is fine; let the question sit, like a lamp in a dark grove.

wordCard.voice: Uposatha. The observance day, at the moon's turning: the night a troubled king rode out to ask what the contemplative life is good for.

orig.note: Pali uposatha: the observance day at the new and full moons. the night the king rode out.

carryVoice: Your line: like a clear lake. Twelve hundred and fifty monks, and not one cough. That's day five hundred twenty-six.
